title: Guidance Note On Cybersecurity For The Insurance Industry
text:

CYBERSECURITY FOR THE
INSURANCE INDUSTRY
JUNE 2025
Insurance Regulatory Authority

PART I: PRELIMINARY
1.1 AUTHORIZATION
IN EXERCISE of the powers conferred by sections 3A (a), (b) and (g) of the
Insurance Act, the Insurance Regulatory Authority (herein referred to as “the
Authority”) issues the Guidance Note set out here below, for observance by all
insurers licensed under the Insurance Act, CAP. 487 Laws of Kenya.
1.2 APPLICATION
This Guidance Note applies to all insurance and reinsurance companies licensed
under the Insurance Act. This Guidance Note is intended to enhance cyber
resilience, safeguard information integrity, and strengthen data protection
across the insurance sector.
1.3 DEFINITIONS
The terms and acronyms used in this Guidance Note are defined below: -
i) Access Controls: Measures and tools used to restrict access to systems, data,
and resources based on user roles and authorization levels.
ii) Artificial Intelligence (AI): Computer systems or software capable of
performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as decision-
making or pattern recognition.
iii) Anti-Malware Protection: Tools or software used to detect, prevent, and
remove malicious software including viruses, ransomware, spyware, and
worms.
iv) Business Continuity: The ability of an insurer to continue delivery of services
and operations following a disruptive incident.
2

v) Business Continuity Management: A process for identifying potential
operational disruptions and implementing plans to ensure ongoing service
delivery during and after such events.
vi) Business Continuity Plan (BCP): Documented procedures that guide an
insurer’s response and recovery from a disruptive event.
vii) Chief Information Security Officer (CISO): A senior executive responsible
for leading and coordinating an institution’s information and cybersecurity
efforts.
viii) Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act: The Kenyan law that provides for
offences relating to computer systems and cybercrime.
ix) Critical Information Infrastructure (CII): Systems or assets whose
disruption would severely impact economic security, public safety, or national
interest.
x) Cyber Assets: Digital assets including software, hardware, systems, and
networks used in business operations.
xi) Cyber Hygiene: Basic practices and protocols followed by users and
institutions to maintain system security and reduce vulnerabilities.
xii) Cyber Risk: The risk of loss or harm resulting from a breach or failure of
information systems.
xiii) Cybersecurity: The practice of protecting systems, networks, and digital
information from cyber threats. (As defined by NIST).
xiv) Cybersecurity Incident: Any event that compromises or has the potential to
compromise the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information
systems. (NIST Special Publication 800-61).
xv) Data Encryption: The process of converting information into a secure format
to prevent unauthorized access during transmission or storage.
xvi) Data Loss Prevention (DLP): Tools and strategies used to prevent
unauthorized access, transfer, or leakage of sensitive data from an
organization’s systems.
xvii) Data Protection Act: The Kenyan law that governs the processing and
protection of personal data.
3

xviii) Designated Cybersecurity Lead: A senior officer responsible for overseeing
the implementation of cybersecurity strategies and incident response.
xix) Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP): A component of the BCP focused on restoring
IT systems and data after disruption.
xx) Enterprise Risk Management (ERM): A comprehensive approach to
managing all risks within an institution, including cyber risk. (COSO/ISACA).
xxi) Firewall: A security system that monitors and controls incoming and
outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules.
xxii) Incident Response Plan (IRP): A documented strategy for detecting,
responding to, and recovering from cybersecurity incidents. (NIST).
xxiii) Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS): Technologies that
monitor network traffic and detect or block suspicious activities.
xxiv) MITRE ATT&CK: A globally recognized framework that categorizes attacker
behaviors, tactics, and techniques observed in real-world incidents.
xxv) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): A security measure that requires
multiple forms of verification before granting access to systems.
xxvi) NIST – The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology.
xxvii) Password Management: Practices and tools used to enforce secure password
creation, use, and periodic renewal.
xxviii) Penetration Testing: Simulated cyberattacks performed to identify
vulnerabilities within an organization’s systems.
xxix) Phishing: A form of cyber fraud where attackers impersonate legitimate
sources to obtain confidential information.
xxx) Ransomware: Malicious software that encrypts data and demands payment
for its release.
xxxi) Security Information and Event Management (SIEM): A technology
platform for real-time analysis of security alerts generated by hardware and
applications.
xxxii) Threat Intelligence: Evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging
cyber threats that can inform detection, response, and mitigation strategies.
4

xxxiii) Vulnerability Scan: An automated process used to identify known
weaknesses in systems or applications.
xxxiv) Zero Trust Architecture: A security model that assumes no implicit trust
and requires continuous authentication, authorization, and validation of
security posture for all users and devices.
5

PART II: STATEMENT OF POLICY
2.1 INTRODUCTION
The insurance sector in Kenya is undergoing rapid digital transformation, driven
by the adoption of emerging technologies to enhance operational efficiency,
customer engagement, and data management. While this shift presents
significant opportunities, it also introduces heightened exposure to cybersecurity
threats and data breaches.
In this regard, safeguarding sensitive information and ensuring the continuity of
critical operations is of strategic importance. Cybersecurity is essential for
preserving operational integrity, regulatory compliance, and maintaining public
confidence in the insurance sector.
Cyber incidents in the insurance industry can significantly affect policyholders
- through the compromise of personal and financial data, disruption of claims
processing, denial of service, or erosion of trust in the institution. As cyber
threats grow in scale and sophistication, it is important for insurers to adopt
proactive and resilient measures to safeguard systems, data, and services.
2.2 PURPOSE
This Guidance Note sets out the minimum standards for the management of
cybersecurity risks within the insurance sector. It aims to promote sound
practices in cybersecurity governance, risk management, and incident response.
2.2.1 Objectives
The key objectives of this Guidance Note are to: -
i) Strengthen institutional governance and accountability for cybersecurity.
6

ii) Enhance the ability of insurers to prevent, detect, respond to, and recover
from cyber incidents.
iii) Support compliance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements,
aligned with international best practices.
iv) Foster public trust and confidence in the insurance sector.
v) Promote a risk-based and adaptive approach to cybersecurity, tailored to the
unique risks and operational contexts of individual insurers.
2.2.2 Scope
This Guidance Note is intended to provide high-level direction and is not
exhaustive, nor does it supersede existing legislative provisions. It should be read
in conjunction with the relevant provisions of the Insurance Act, its subsidiary
legislation, and any circulars, notices, or guidelines issued by the Authority or
other competent authorities.
2.3 RESPONSIBILITY
The ultimate responsibility for an insurer’s cybersecurity framework rests with
the Board of Directors and senior management. Insurers are expected to develop
and implement cybersecurity strategies, policies, and procedures appropriate to
their size, complexity, and risk exposure.
These documents should be formally approved, reviewed regularly, and made
available for examination by internal and external auditors and the Authority.
7

2.4 SOURCES OF CYBER RISK
Cyber risk in the insurance industry can originate from a variety of internal and
external sources, including but not limited to: -
i) Cyberattacks: Malicious acts such as ransomware, phishing, denial-of-
service attacks (DoS) and advanced persistent threats (APTs).
ii) Insider Threats: Intentional or unintentional actions by employees or
affiliates that result in data breaches (e.g., unauthorized data sharing), fraud
(e.g., manipulating policy or claims data), or operational disruption (e.g.,
accidental deletion of critical files, misuse of system privileges).
iii) Third-Party Risks: These arise from service providers or contractors whose
systems, networks, or processes may be vulnerable to cyber threats,
potentially impacting the insurer's operations or data security.
iv) Technological Vulnerabilities: Risks associated with outdated software,
unpatched systems, and misconfigured networks that could be exploited by
cybercriminals.
v) AI-Specific Risks - Even basic AI tools (e.g., chatbots, claims automation)
could lead to unclear decision-making, data leaks, or unfair bias if poorly
managed. Even as AI adoption accelerates, weak governance today might
embed these vulnerabilities into future systems.
8

PART III: SPECIFIC REQUIREMENTS
3.1 CYBERSECURITY STRATEGY
Insurers are expected to establish and maintain a documented cybersecurity
strategy that is proportionate to their size, nature, and complexity. The strategy
should articulate clear objectives, delineate roles and responsibilities, and
describe the tools, processes, and capabilities required to manage cyber risk.
While insurers may adopt internationally recognized cybersecurity standards
(e.g., NIST, ISO/IEC 27001), the strategy must be aligned with relevant national
legislation, including the Data Protection Act, 2019; the Computer Misuse and
Cybercrimes Act, 2018; and any guidelines issued by the Authority or other
competent authorities.
Insurers should adopt Zero Trust Architecture principles to minimize implicit
trust across their systems and networks. This includes enforcing strict identity
verification, least privilege access, and continuous monitoring. For insurers
leveraging cloud environments, security strategies should incorporate Cloud
Access Security Brokers (CASBs) and workload identity management to ensure
consistent control enforcement.
The cybersecurity strategy should be subject to regular review, at a minimum
annually, or upon the occurrence of a significant incident, introduction of new
systems, or material changes in the cyber threat landscape.
The strategy should be approved by the Board of Directors and communicated
across the institution, including periodic awareness for staff on the strategic
direction.
9

3.2 GOVERNANCE
Cybersecurity governance requires a clearly defined and well-coordinated
structure involving the Board of Directors, Senior Management, and the
Designated Cybersecurity Lead. Each level plays a distinct but complementary
role in ensuring a secure and resilient technology environment.
3.2.1 Board of Directors
The Board of Directors bears overall responsibility for an insurer’s cybersecurity
governance. It is expected to demonstrate leadership by fostering a proactive
culture of cyber risk awareness and ensuring that cybersecurity is integrated
into the organization’s strategic agenda. The Board’s duties shall include, but
not limited to: -
i) Approving and overseeing the cybersecurity strategy, policy, and governance
framework.
ii) Defining the institution’s cyber risk appetite and tolerance limits, and
ensuring integration with overall risk management practices.
iii) Promoting a culture of cybersecurity awareness and ethical behavior.
iv) Ensuring adequate financial, human, and technological resources are
allocated for cybersecurity functions.
v) Establishing governance structures that support effective oversight, including
the appointment of a qualified individual to oversee cybersecurity. This
individual may serve as the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) or
equivalent role, and should report to the Board or its committee on a regular
basis, ensuring independent oversight.
vi) Receiving timely reports on cyber threats and incidents and ensure that
appropriate corrective actions are taken.
vii) Ensuring cybersecurity is a standing item on the Board’s agenda, particularly
in relation to major ICT investments or outsourcing arrangements.
10

viii) Ensuring continuous training or access to expert advice for the Board to
remain informed on cyber-related issues.
Boards are further encouraged to include at least one member with relevant
experience or knowledge in technology or cybersecurity to enhance oversight
effectiveness.
3.2.2 Senior Management
Senior Management is responsible for translating the Board-approved
cybersecurity strategy into effective organizational practices. This entails
overseeing implementation, coordination, and resourcing of cybersecurity
functions across all operational levels. Responsibilities include: -
i) Developing and operationalizing cybersecurity procedures in line with
approved policies.
ii) Embedding robust controls into business operations to support cyber risk
mitigation.
iii) Establishing capacity for detecting, managing, and escalating cybersecurity
incidents in a timely and coordinated manner.
iv) Keeping the Board informed on cybersecurity risks, performance indicators
(e.g., number of security incidents, time to detect and respond), and incident
trends.
v) Implementing technical safeguards such as secure authentication, logical
access controls, and data protection mechanisms to ensure system and
customer data integrity.
vi) Managing third-party cybersecurity risk through due diligence, contractual
safeguards, and ongoing monitoring.
vii) Embedding cybersecurity awareness across departments and functions,
supported by recurring training and scenario-based drills e.g., phishing drills,
social engineering tactics, and other common attack vectors.
11

viii) Ensuring the institution is adequately staffed with skilled and vetted
cybersecurity personnel.
ix) Ensuring institutional compliance with applicable laws and data protection
obligations, including registration with regulatory bodies where necessary.
x) Ensuring cybersecurity performance metrics such as mean time to
detect/respond (MTTD/MTTR), open vulnerabilities, and patch management
delays should be reviewed monthly by senior management. Any material risks
or trends must be reported to the Board with recommendations for corrective
action.
3.2.3 Designated Cybersecurity Lead
Insurers are expected to designate a senior individual with overall responsibility
for cybersecurity. Depending on the institution’s scale and complexity, this may
be: -
• A dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO); or
• An existing senior officer with appropriate cybersecurity expertise and
independence.
The individual should hold a senior position with sufficient authority and
independence, reporting functionally to the Board or its designated committee
and administratively to the Principal Officer. Key responsibilities shall at a
minimum include: -
i) Driving execution of the institution’s cybersecurity strategy and ensuring
implementation across all departments.
ii) Providing technical leadership in the design and upkeep of security
architecture, including preventative and detective mechanisms
12

iii) Leading the formulation, maintenance, and testing of the institution’s
incident response framework to ensure operational readiness in the event of
a cyberattack.
iv) Coordinating internal and external responses to cybersecurity incidents, and
ensuring lessons learned are incorporated into future strategies.
v) Advising senior executives and the Board on cyber risk trends, vulnerabilities,
and investment needs to strengthen organizational resilience.
vi) Managing awareness campaigns, technical training, and staff guidance
initiatives to elevate cyber hygiene across the institution.
vii) Overseeing the cybersecurity risk profile of external vendors and ensuring
that service providers operate in line with established standards.
3.3 RISK MANAGEMENT
Insurers are expected to adopt a structured and proactive approach to
cybersecurity risk management in line with their risk appetite and strategic
goals. Cyber risk should be integrated into the institution’s overall enterprise
risk management (ERM) framework, with appropriate governance, systems, and
processes to support timely identification, assessment, mitigation, and
monitoring of risks arising from cyber threats.
3.3.1 Cyber Risk Identification and Assessment
Insurers should identify cyber risks and conduct assessment on the effectiveness
of the mitigating measures to protect against and manage cyber risks within the
risk appetite and tolerance limit set by the Board. This assessment should
consider both internal and external sources of risk, potential impact, and
likelihood of occurrence, considering the interconnectedness of systems and
potential cascading impacts. The risk identification and assessment shall
include: -
13

i) Conducting regular threat assessments and vulnerability scans to identify
weaknesses.
ii) Comprehensive risk assessments, including scenario-based analyses to
evaluate potential impacts.
iii) Identification and prioritization of critical assets, including data,
infrastructure, and services crucial to operations and compliance obligations.
iv) Maintaining a dynamic cyber risk register that reflects current exposures,
vulnerabilities, and control gaps.
v) Analyzing both internal and external sources of risk, including supply chains,
AI dependencies, and evolving threat actors.
vi) Performing periodic red teaming and adversary emulation exercises to test
the effectiveness of controls and detection capabilities. Key findings should
be documented and used to update the institution’s cyber risk register and
security strategies.
3.3.2 Risk Mitigation and Controls
Insurers should implement appropriate controls based on the outcomes of their
risk assessments. Essential controls include, but are not limited to:
i) Access Controls: User access to systems, data, and facilities should be strictly
controlled, ensuring that individuals are granted only the minimum level of
access necessary to perform their assigned duties, in line with the principle
of least privilege.
ii) Network Security: Deploy firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), and
intrusion prevention systems (IPS).
iii) Anti-Malware Protection: Ensure comprehensive endpoint protection.
iv) Data Encryption: Apply strong encryption standards to protect sensitive data
both in transit and at rest.
14

v) Security Configuration Management: Enforce secure configuration baselines
and timely patching of software and hardware vulnerabilities.
vi) Continuous Monitoring: Establish real-time monitoring capabilities (Security
Information and Event Management - SIEM) to detect anomalous activities
and respond promptly to incidents.
vii) Security Audits: Conduct regular audits and penetration testing.
Institutions should also align their defensive strategies with internationally
recognized frameworks such as the MITRE ATT&CK Matrix, which maps out real-
world attacker tactics and techniques. Integration with cyber threat intelligence
feeds is recommended to enhance detection of evolving threats and enable a
proactive defense posture.
3.3.3 Cyber Hygiene and User Awareness
Insurers should establish foundational cyber hygiene practices and foster a
culture of cybersecurity awareness across the organization, such as:
i) Password Management: Mandate strong, unique passwords and periodically
require their update. Implement password complexity requirements and
discourage the reuse of passwords.
ii) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Implement MFA, especially for
administrative and critical system access.
iii) Regular Software Updates: Maintain an updated inventory of software assets
and ensure timely patching of identified vulnerabilities.
iv) Employee Training: Conduct regular cybersecurity awareness programs
addressing phishing, social engineering, malware, data security policies, and
other emerging threats.
v) Secure Backup Procedures: Ensure regular and secure backups of critical
data to support business continuity and disaster recovery. Regularly test
backup and recovery processes.
15

3.3.4 Incident Response and Business Continuity Management
Insurers are required to develop, maintain, and regularly test a comprehensive
Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan (CIRP). The CIRP should:
i) Clearly define roles, responsibilities, and communication channels for
incident handling and escalation.
ii) Include procedures for containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident
review.
iii) Establish protocols for timely notification to the Authority and other relevant
bodies as required by law.
iv) Integrate with broader Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plans,
ensuring resilience in the face of cyber incidents.
v) Conduct biannual simulation exercises (e.g., tabletop testing or red/blue
team exercises) to assess the effectiveness of the Cybersecurity Incident
Response Plan (CIRP). Each simulation must be followed by a formal lesson
learned review, with updates incorporated into the CIRP and training
materials.
3.3.5 Third Party Risk Management
Recognizing the growing interdependence between insurers and external parties,
particularly in areas such as data processing, cloud services, and technology
solutions, insurers should: -
i) Conduct due diligence assessments of third-party cybersecurity capabilities
and compliance before engagement.
ii) Include cybersecurity requirements (aligned with the insurer’s own
standards) in contractual agreements with service providers, including
service level agreements (SLAs) related to security and incident response.
iii) Regularly monitor third-party cybersecurity practices and performance.
16

iv) Develop exit management strategies and contingency plans.
v) Ensure third parties AI tools are transparent, secure and governed
appropriately. Have signed contracts that must include:
a) Mandatory breach notification clauses.
b) Right-to-audit provisions.
c) Minimum security baseline requirements, aligned with the insurer’s
internal standards.
3.3.6 Reporting and Monitoring
Insurers are expected to establish effective reporting and monitoring systems:
i) Regularly report cybersecurity risks and incidents to the Board and senior
management.
ii) Develop metrics and indicators to monitor cybersecurity posture and
effectiveness of controls.
iii) Provide periodic cybersecurity reports to the Authority upon request.
iv) Subject cybersecurity controls and frameworks to regular internal and
external audits, with findings reported independently to the Board.
v) Ensure all critical infrastructure systems undergo an independent third-party
cybersecurity audit at least annually. The results shall be submitted to the
Board and summarized in the annual cybersecurity assurance report
submitted to the Authority.
17

PART IV: REPORTING
4.1 SUBMISSION AND REVIEW OF CYBERSECURITY FRAMEWORK
Each insurer is required to develop and maintain a comprehensive Cybersecurity
Policy and supporting framework aligned with this Guidance Note. The
Cybersecurity Policy shall be submitted to the Authority within 14 days from the
date it is approved by the Board or upon request by the Authority.
Insurers should internally review and update their cybersecurity policy at least
annually, or upon significant changes in their ICT environment, threat
landscape, or regulatory obligations. Re-submission to the Authority shall only
be required upon written request or as directed following material changes.
The minimum elements expected within a Cybersecurity Policy are outlined in
Annex I of this Guidance Note.
4.2 NOTIFICATION OF CRITICAL CYBERSECURITY EVENTS
All material cybersecurity incidents with potential to significantly impact service
delivery, reputation, operations, or financial stability must be reported to the
Authority within 24 hours from confirmation or substantiated detection,
whichever is earlier.
A cybersecurity incident shall be deemed material if it: -
i) Causes significant disruption of critical services, platforms, or systems.
ii) Results in or is suspected to result in unauthorized access, loss, or disclosure
of sensitive, personal, or customer information.
iii) Leads to or may lead to financial loss to the insurer, its clients, or third
parties.
18

iv) Involves high-impact threats such as malware, ransomware, denial of service
(DoS).
v) Poses a risk to public confidence or may undermine the reputation of the
insurer or the broader insurance sector.
Notifications shall be made using the prescribed format provided in Annex II.
4.3 QUARTERLY INCIDENT REPORTING
To maintain a comprehensive understanding of the cybersecurity incident
landscape within the insurance sector, each insurer is required to submit a
quarterly report to the Authority within fifteen (15) days of the end of the quarter
to which it relates. This report should detail all cybersecurity incidents that
occurred during the preceding three-month period, along with a summary of
their handling and resolution. The specific format for this quarterly submission
is provided in Annex III (Quarterly) of this Guidance Note.
4.4 SPECIFIC INFORMATION REQUESTS
The Authority may issue ad hoc requests for information or clarification
regarding an insurer’s cybersecurity posture, threat exposure, or incident
response. Insurers are required to provide complete and timely responses within
the stipulated timelines.
All reports and submissions should be transmitted securely to the Authority
via the designated email: returns@ira.go.ke.
19

For further inquiries, insurers may contact:
The Director Supervision,
Insurance Regulatory Authority
P. O. Box 43505 - 00100
Nairobi
Telephone: +254 20 4996000
Email: supervision@ira.go.ke
20

ANNEX I: HIGH LEVEL CONTENTS OF A CYBERSECURITY POLICY
The Cybersecurity Policy should generally contain, at a minimum, the following:
-
a) Governance - Mechanisms established to implement, oversee, and
periodically review the organization's cybersecurity management approach.
b) Cybersecurity Objectives – Clearly defined goals aimed at safeguarding
organizational assets, ensuring continuity, and maintaining compliance with
relevant laws.
c) Risk Management Framework – Structured processes for identifying,
assessing, prioritizing, and mitigating cybersecurity risks in alignment with
the organization’s risk appetite. This should include the maintenance of a risk
register.
d) Access and Identity Management – Procedures and controls for managing
user identities and access, ensuring users have only necessary privileges to
perform their roles.
e) Information Protection – Standards and processes established for
classifying, handling, and protecting sensitive and critical organizational
data.
f) Security Controls and Technology – Technical and administrative
safeguards deployed across systems and networks to protect against
cybersecurity threats.
g) Incident Management and Response – Clearly defined protocols and
responsibilities for detecting, responding to, managing, and recovering from
cybersecurity incidents.
h) Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery – Plans designed to maintain
critical business functions during disruptions and to swiftly recover IT
systems post-incident.
i) Third-party Cybersecurity Risk Management – Framework for evaluating,
managing, and monitoring cybersecurity risks posed by third-party vendors
and service providers.

j) Training and Awareness – Programs and initiatives to ensure employees and
stakeholders are educated and informed about cybersecurity threats and best
practices.
k) Monitoring, Audits, and Compliance – Processes established for ongoing
cybersecurity monitoring, regular audits, and compliance verification to
uphold policy effectiveness.
l) Policy Maintenance and Review – Procedures for regularly reviewing,
updating, and maintaining the cybersecurity policy to ensure ongoing
relevance and effectiveness.

title: IC/04/2011 circular on lein 0f 28th June 2011.
text:
CONF/IRA/00/001/03
28th June, 2011
CIRCULAR NO. IC/04/2011
TO: ALL INSURERS, RE-INSURERS, INSURANCE BROKERS AND MEDICAL
INSURANCE PROVIDERS
RE: CENTRAL BANK FUNDS HELD UNDER LIEN
Reference is made to our circular No. IC/03/2003 dated 17th October 2003 regarding
submission of lien applications to the Insurance Regulatory Authority.
We have noted that insurers continue to submit lien applications late hence not giving
us enough time to scrutinize the documents before approval.
To improve this process, you are hereby advised that all lien applications MUST be
submitted to the Insurance Regulatory Authority at least seven days (7) before due
date.
The applications should be on the usual CDS forms (where applicable) with a
covering letter and a schedule showing the existing liens and their expiry dates.
Please be guided accordingly.
SAMMY M. MAKOVE
COMMISSIONER OF INSURANCE & CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER

title: Insurance Industry Prudential Guidelines 2008
text:
CIRCULARS TO THE INSURANCE INDUSTRY
IC & RE 10/2008: policy As per provisions of section 30 of the Insurance Act, insurers are
documents wordings
required to submit copies of proposal and policy forms,
endorsements and any form of written matter describing the terms
or conditions of or the benefit to or likely to be derived from
policies that are issued by the insurer.
We have however noted that some insurers have been using
policy/proposal/endorsement wordings which have not been
approved by this office.
For this reason, you are required to submit copies of all proposal
forms, policy documents and endorsements currently in use for
the following classes of business:
 Aviation
 Personal Accident
 Motor Private
 Motor Commercial
 Theft
 Liability and
 Marine
This information should be submitted not later than 31st
December, 2008.
Premium rates for listed risks were reviewed last in year 2005.
IC & RE 09/2008: Premium
rates for listed risks Since then, insurers have continued to file the same rates.
I recently appointed a Risk Evaluation Committee to look into the
appropriateness of these rates and recommend the way forward.
In order to check on compliance with the filed rates, I also
requested insurance companies vide my Circular dated 2nd July
2008 to submit to this office rates applied on all listed risks. An
audit of the applied rates has revealed that:-
i. The majority of risks are rated well below (some times up
to 50%) the filed (base) rates disclosing massive
undercutting.
ii. The existing thresholds for the listed risks of Kshs.300
million for fire risks and Kshs.150 million for engineering
risks are considered appropriate.
iii. That the 2005 summary of listed risks was correctly rated
and the rates were intended to be base rates that required
to be enhanced in phases to technical rates within a period

iv. That new risks in this bracket have not been evaluated to

In view of the above, I wish to urgently draw your attention to the

 That we still maintain the 2005 recommended rates for

 That new risks (Exceeding the thresholds) not appearing

 All underwriters are required to apply premium rates filed

 A copy of the rates filed with this office should be given
to the re-insurers for information.

November 2008.
