2.12 Tax Crimes ML Risks
The Kenyan tax system is a self-assessment system where a taxpayer assesses himself
or herself and makes payments to the revenue authority. However, some individuals or
business entities abuse the trust bestowed on them by the law by under declaring or
failing to declare their income, hence evading payment of taxes.
The tax crimes ML risk in Kenya is assessed as Medium. The ML threat from tax crimes
is rated Medium High, while the overall vulnerability to tax crimes is assessed as
Medium Low due to the strong control system in place.
The assessment focused on the major schemes prevalent in Kenya. These schemes are
divided into tax crime schemes and ML schemes as highlighted below:
2.12.1 Common tax related crimes in Kenya
The main types of tax crimes identified in the country are described below:
i. VAT carrousel fraud/Missing trader schemes
Refers to establishment of shell companies that are not trading but issue tax
invoices, to enable trading companies claim expenses, in order to reduce tax
liability. This typology contributed to 70% of cases reviewed.
The Financial Reporting Centre 25

Money Laundering National Risk Assessment Guidance
ii. Use of power of attorney/nominees/directorships to hide the beneficial owner
of a legal structure
This takes place through layering, direct ownership chains, as well as
professional intermediaries and third parties exercising control on behalf of the
beneficial owners. This typology contributed to 20% of cases reviewed.
iii. Multi-jurisdiction structuring
Refers to creation of financial structures/legal entities across multiple
jurisdictions to hide financial transactions and evade payment of taxes. This
typology contributed to 6% of cases reviewed.
iv. Recording income as loans or other non-taxable income
Residents make income, which should be declared for tax purposes, but transfer
the income to a third party who transfers back the money as a loan to the
resident. The resident declares the income as a loan from the third party hence
evading payment of taxes. This typology contributed to 2% of cases reviewed
v. Abuse of charitable organizations
This occurs where residents register charitable organizations and use them to
hide taxable income. This typology contributed to 1% of cases reviewed.
vi. Electronic sales suppression
This involves operating parallel electronic tax invoicing systems and declaring
only one. This typology contributed to 0.4% of cases reviewed.
vii. Income in nominee name; hidden bank accounts
A beneficial owner hides assets by employing a nominee to make purchases
and hold assets. Nominee here is a mere custodian who hands over assets to
the actual owner. This typology contributed to 0.2% of cases reviewed.
viii. Offshore asset concealment
Residents repatriate locally acquired income and assets to offshore
jurisdictions, without declaring the same locally. This typology contributed to
0.2% of cases reviewed.
The Financial Reporting Centre 26

Money Laundering National Risk Assessment Guidance
ix. Unreported bank accounts in non-cooperative countries
Residents open bank accounts in offshore jurisdictions and do not declare the
accounts. This typology contributed to 0.2% of cases reviewed.
2.12.2 Tax crimes related ML typologies
The main tax crimes-related money laundering typologies identified are described
below:
i. Use of power of attorney and nominees
This typology takes place through layering, direct ownership chains, as well as
professional intermediaries and third parties exercising control on behalf of the
beneficial owners. The typology contributed to 52% of cases reviewed.
ii. Trade based money laundering
This involves the use of trade transactions in an attempt to legitimize the origins
of proceeds of crime. The scheme contributed about 34% of all reviewed cases.
iii. Purchase of high-value assets
This involves acquisition of high value assets for purposes of hiding of proceeds
of crime. The number of cases reviewed are 10% of the total reviewed cases.
iv. Abuse of trust and company service providers
The use of trust and company service providers wittingly or unwittingly, in the
conduct of money laundering activities, contributed to 4% of the cases reviewed.
v. Wire transfers
A wire transfer is an electronic transfer of funds via a network that is
administered by banks and transfer service agencies around the world.
Residents use wire transfers to move illicit cash from one jurisdiction to another.
Some financial institutions collude with unscrupulous residents to transfer huge
sums of money from one tax jurisdiction to another without the knowledge of
regulatory agencies. This scheme contributed to 1% of the cases reviewed.
The Financial Reporting Centre 27

Money Laundering National Risk Assessment Guidance
APPENDIX: ML RELATED CASE TYPOLOGIES
1. Foreign Predicates
Case example 1: Repatriating recovered proceeds to Tanzania
In July 2019, Kenyan Government repatriated gold worth about KES 168 million and more than KES 15
million (in cash) to the Tanzanian Authorities. Earlier in March 2018, LEAs in Kenya and Tanzania
collaborated to intercept and recover the said items from a suspect who was arrested at the Jomo Kenyatta
International Airport. Investigations revealed that the recovered gold was part of a heist from Tanzania’s
National Bank of Commerce (NBC) in Moshi, alongside more than KES 180 million cash in US Dollars,
Kenyan shillings and Tanzanian shillings. The prime suspect, P.A.N, was also later arrested in Kenya
and repatriated to Tanzania for prosecution in January 2019.
During the handover of the recovered items, the President of Kenya, Mr. Uhuru Kenyatta, said the
following to Tanzanian President Mr. John Pombe Magufuli, on phone, “My brother, I say we continue
working together and Kenya and Tanzania has no borders as we agreed. We should help one another to
fight corruption and to return money stolen from our people so that we build roads and connect our
people to electricity.”
Case example 2: Chickengate scandal
This was a case involving bribery of English nationals in the procurement of contracts for supply of ballot
papers. It started with the payout of millions of shillings in what the Courts in the United Kingdom
described as bribes to Kenyan election officials by a British company. The illicit deals were carried out
under the code name ‘chicken’ essentially to award lucrative printing contracts. The UK through National
Crime Agency conducted investigations resulting in two Englishmen being tried and convicted under the
English Bribery Act and confiscation orders made. The Company was also found guilty and fined £2.2
million.
Kenya recovered KES 52 million from the “Chickengate” scandal, which the Ethics and Anti- Corruption
Commission (EACC) confirmed was part of proceedings to repatriate assets of the London-based
security printer. The repatriated funds were later used to buy seven (7) ambulances that were distributed
to vulnerable areas through the Ministry of Health.
Case example 3: Framework for the return of assets from crime and corruption in Kenya (FRACCK)
The Framework for the return of assets from crime and corruption in Kenya (FRACCK) was signed by
the Government of the Republic of Kenya, the Swiss Federal Council, the Government of the United
Kingdom and the Government of Jersey, to provide the framework for effective and expeditious
repatriation of proceeds of crime and corruption that have been illegally transferred in other jurisdictions.
In 2022, the Government of Jersey and Kenya reached an agreement for repatriation of £3 million to
support Kenya's Government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The funds were confiscated by
Jersey authorities in 2016, following the successful conviction of Windward Trading Ltd. for money
laundering offences.
Case example 4: Multi-jurisdiction structuring of funds and Trade-based Money Laundering
The scheme involved an established company in Kenya (subject company) owned by a shell company
registered in a tax haven outside Kenya, which is further owned by another company based in a third
country. The shell company registered in the tax haven country advanced loans to the Kenyan company
at an agreed interest rate. The Kenyan company has a sister company in Kenya involved in manufacturing.
The sister company sold its products to the subject Kenyan company which was involved in distribution
of the products to the market.
The sister company through its employees registered other companies in Kenya and opened bank
accounts in the names of those other companies. The registered owners of these companies were Kenyans
but the account signatories were employees of the sister company. These other companies did not trade
but had huge sums of money deposited in their bank accounts held in various banks in Kenya. The money
was deposited in both cash and cheques. The cash deposits were made by employees of the subject
taxpayer. The subject company requested some customers to write cheques in favour of the associated
local companies that were then deposited in their accounts. The money was then transferred to the dollar
The Financial Reporting Centre 28

Money Laundering National Risk Assessment Guidance
denominated accounts held by the same companies before being wired to the holding company in the
third country purportedly to purchase stock.
The subject company did not declare income corresponding with diverted funds. Examination of customs
database indicated that these companies never imported any goods. Therefore, the transfer of cash to the
holding company could not have been for purchase of stock. In the end, the products manufactured by
the sister company in Kenya was sold to the subject company which subsequently sold the same without
reporting the sales for tax purposes and transferred the cash to the holding company outside Kenya to
conceal the non-declaration.
The tax crime typology deployed in this case, include creation of multi-jurisdiction structuring of funds,
local structuring using hidden accounts in the name of associated entities, TBML, using employees to
register companies to hide beneficial ownership as well as reporting income as related party foreign loans.
Case example 5: Foreign structuring through legal structures
Company Y registered in country M owned 100% shareholding of company Z also registered in the same
country M. Z owns 100% shareholding of company ZZ registered in Kenya. Y disposed 30% of its
shareholding in Z to company A, registered in country F at KES 5.2 billion. Based on the information
shared by the tax administration in country M, it was established that the directors of Y are also the
directors of ZZ. The directors are resident in Kenya and exercise control of the affairs and business of Y
from Kenya. Consequently, Y was obligated under section 15 of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 to appoint
a tax representative in Kenya to file returns and pay taxes in Kenya. By failing to do so, KRA appointed
ZZ as Y’s tax representative and issued it with tax assessment of KES 1.8 billion. The whole arrangement
was designed to defeat the tax system. Y disputed the assessment and subsequently appealed the KRA’s
objection decision to the Tax Appeals Tribunal (TAT). TAT issued a judgment on the matter in August
2023, dismissing the appeal in favour of KRA.
The typology used in this case was multi-jurisdiction structuring where resident individuals used legal
structures registered in other jurisdictions to conceal disposal of part of the shareholding in their local
company to another entity registered in a different jurisdiction and failed to pay Capital Gains Tax arising
from the transaction.
Case example 6: Foreign structuring through legal arrangements
X, which is registered in Kenya as a limited liability partnership, purchased about 452 million shares in
B holdings limited, resident in Kenya from a non-resident entity registered in country M. It later sold off
the shares in two transactions realizing some gains from the overall transaction. The partners of X did
not declare the profit in their individual income tax returns. According to section 3 of the Income Tax
Act, a partnership is not a taxable person hence the requirement for partners to declare partnership profits
in the profit sharing ratios and pay the corresponding taxes. X has two partners, an individual and an
incorporated entity in company M. This income was brought to charge on both persons as business
income since the purpose for the formation of the partnership was to invest funds provided by partners.
The KRA investigated the matter and obtained information and evidence from country M, regarding the
legal ownership, BO and bank information, to finalize the case. An assessment amounting to KES 1.575
billion was issued to the partners for taxes not paid. This typology concerns a multi-jurisdiction
structuring involving Kenya and country M, as well as the use of non-taxable special purpose vehicles,
that is limited liability partnerships, to execute the transactions and evade taxation.
2. Banking Sector
Case example 7:
Investigations were guided by a dissemination from the Centre that led to the arrest of three suspects for
Acquisition of Proceeds of Crime Contrary to Section 4(a) as read with Section 16(1) (a) of the
POCAMLA. The accused persons registered 19 mobile accounts using several ID cards belonging to
unsuspecting individuals and jointly received KES 37,821,548 from international money transfer. They
eventually withdrew the same through two AB till numbers, AG Bank, AF Bank, AA Bank and AS Bank.
The mater is still ongoing in Court.
3. Money Value Transfer Services (Mobile Money)
The Financial Reporting Centre 29

Money Laundering National Risk Assessment Guidance
Case example 8: Abuse of MVTS
Investigations were guided by a dissemination from FRC which led to the arrest of one suspect by the
name BD. He was charged with the offence of acquisition of proceeds of crime contrary to Section 4(a)
as read with Section 16(1) (a) of the POCAMLA. Investigations revealed that the accused person
collected several ID cards from his relatives located within BXX region in Kenya and fraudulently used
them to register sim cards which he eventually used to receive money from Country BG. 10 sim cards
were used to receive a total of KES 11,293,474, and withdrawn through 41 BY till numbers. The matter
is still ongoing in Court.
Case example 9:
Investigations were guided by a dissemination from FRC which led to the arrest of two suspects CMM
and CXK. The accused persons were charged with the offence of Acquisition of Proceeds of Crime
Contrary to Section 4(a) as read with Section 16(1) (a) of the Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money
Laundering Act. CMM received a total of KES 8,794,189 through two CG accounts numbers
07xxxxxx30 and 07xxxxxx04. The said amounts were later withdrawn using two CY till numbers, all
registered under CW Ltd. CXK received a total of KES 1,462,314 using two CG accounts 07xxxxxx91
and 07xxxxxx29 and later withdrew through CY till number registered under CZ Ltd. The matter was
heard and the suspects were convicted and fined.
4. Money Remittance Providers
Case example 10:
Two suspects were charged with the offence of acquisition of proceeds of crime contrary to section 4(a)
as read with section 16(1) (a) of POCAMLA. Investigations revealed that both accused persons were
ABC MMSP till operators, agents and mobile phone subscribers. They registered several telephone
numbers using their ID cards and other ID cards belonging to unsuspecting individuals. The accused
persons fraudulently used the above numbers to register MMSP accounts which eventually received
money from HYD, MNP Money and International Money Transfer from Country GX.
Suspect one received a total of KES 13,482,751 through ABC MMSP telephone numbers which he
eventually withdrew locally through a till number. Suspect two received a total of KES 18,794,307
through several MMSP accounts. He eventually withdrew cash through the several till numbers. Apart
from the till numbers, HGT Bank and BTD Bank accounts were used to transfer money from the above
till numbers and eventual withdraws. The accused persons were convicted and fined.
Case example 11:
Investigations were guided by an intelligence report from FRC which led to the arrest of two accused
persons who were refugees at BB Camp. They were charged with the offence of Acquisition of proceeds
of crime contrary to Section 4(a) as read with Section 16(1) (a) of the POCAMLA. Investigations
revealed that both accused persons received money through GHB International money transfer, BGS
money transfer and FTR rated money transfer and international Money transfers from South Africa.
The 1st accused person, through his phone number received a total of KES 1,486,039 from unidentified
persons in country WW while the 2nd accused person received KES 487,804 through his phone number.
Further investigations revealed that the 2nd accused person, jointly with AX, a suspect still at large,
received KES 3,599,000 through KGT Bank account number. The suspects were convicted and fined.

Glossary
AML Compliance Programme refers to the measures put in place by an
institution to prevent, detect, and report instances of money laundering,
terrorist financing and proliferation financing.
Authority refers to the Insurance Regulatory Authority.
Beneficial Owner refers to the natural person (s) who ultimately owns or
controls a legal person or arrangements or the natural person on whose behalf
a transaction is conducted and includes those persons who exercise ultimate
effective control over a legal person or arrangement.
Business-based Risk Assessment (BbRA) refers to the process of identifying,
assessing and understanding ML/TF/PF risks at institutional level to
determine the level of ML/TF/PF risk its operations and related party
activities i.e. the threats, vulnerabilities, and possible consequences.
Centre refers to the Financial Reporting Centre.
Competent authorities refer to public authorities including financial sector
supervisors, with designated responsibilities for combating ML/TF/PF.
Consequence refers to the impact or extent of the damage that may be caused
when a threat exploits vulnerability i.e. when the ML/TF/PF risk materializes.
Emerging risks refer to recently identified but not fully explored ML/TF/PF
threats or vulnerabilities or other phenomena. Previously identified risks that
become apparent in new or unfamiliar conditions can also be considered
emerging risks.
Gatekeeper refers to professionals such as lawyers, notaries, accountants,
investment advisors, and trust and company service providers who assist in
transactions involving the movement of money.
Inherent risk refers to the exposure to ML/TF/PF risk prior to the application
of controls or mitigation measures.
Internal controls refer to Policies, procedures, systems and personnel
designed to protect against the materialisation of a ML/TF/PF risk, or to
ensure that risk factors are promptly identified.

Institutional risk assessment refers to a comprehensive review and
evaluation of the potential ML, TF and PF risks that an institution may be

Likelihood refers to the possibility of ML/TF/PF risk being present.
Material change refers to a shift in an event, activity or situation that has
been identified that could lead to an alteration of the determined level of
ML/TF/PF risk.
Money laundering refers to the process of disguising the existence, source,
movement, destination or illegal application of illegally acquired property or
funds to make them appear legitimate.
Money laundering / terrorist financing / proliferation financing risk
refers to the possibility that an institution, or a product or service offered by
an institution may be used to facilitate ML/TF/PF.
ML/TF/PF risk assessment refers to the process by which an institution
evaluates the extent to which it is vulnerable to ML/TF/PF and the strength
of the controls put in place to mitigate the identified risks.
Politically Exposed Person refers to a person who has been entrusted with
a prominent public function in a country or jurisdiction including—
a) members of Cabinet.
b) senior executives of state owned corporations;
c) important political party officials;
d) senior military officials and other members of the disciplined forces;
e) members of the Judiciary.
f) senior State Officers.
g) senior Public Officers.
h) senior Official of an International Organisation.
i) any immediate family member or close business associate; and
j) any other category of persons as the Centre may determine.
Predicate offences refer to crimes that generate proceeds that need to be

weight to the risk factors based on various factors such as the customer’s
profile, nature of the product / service, mode of delivery of the product /

1.0 Introduction
1.1 Money laundering (ML), terrorist financing (TF) and proliferation
financing (PF) of weapons of mass destruction pose significant
threats to the integrity of economic and financial systems.
1.2 Institutional Risk Assessment (IRA) is an important element and
tool of an institution’s Anti-Money Laundering (AML)1 compliance
programme.
1.3 An IRA is a comprehensive review and evaluation of the potential
money laundering (ML), terrorist financing (TF) and proliferation
financing (PF) risks that a reporting institution2 may be exposed to.
1.4 An IRA identifies the range of risks impacting a reporting
institution’s operations.
1.5 A risk-based approach (RBA) is central to the effective
implementation of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF)
Recommendations3.
1.6 The focus on risk is to enable institutions to identify, assess and
understand the ML, TF and PF risks to which they are exposed and
take appropriate measures to mitigate the identified risks.
1.7 RBA facilitates allocation of resources to areas of heightened risks
to mitigate against ML, TF, PF and other financial crimes.
1.8 The purpose of conducting an IRA is to:
1.8.1 Identify, assess and measure ML, TF and PF risks an
institution is exposed to.
1.8.2 Understand the risks to which the institution is exposed.
1.8.3 Facilitate development and implementation controls to manage
and mitigate risks identified.
1.8.4 Ensure full compliance with the legislation.
1.8.5 Increase the focus on the products or services, transactions,
customers, geographic locations and delivery channels that are
more vulnerable to abuse by money launderers, terrorist
financiers and other criminals.
1.8.6 Ensure that the ML, TF and PF risks are assessed and
mitigated before new products/services are offered.
1.8.7 Implement enhanced controls where higher risks are identified.
1 AML Compliance Programme includes measures put in place to combat terrorist financing
and proliferation financing.
2 In this guidance note, ‘Reporting Institution(s)’ and ‘Institution(s)’ are used interchangeably.
3 The FATF Recommendations set out a comprehensive and consistent framework of
measures which countries should implement to combat money laundering, terrorist financing
and financing of proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.

1.9 IRA is the tool used by institutions to identify, assess and understand
the risks faced in the different areas of their business.
1.10 The outcome of the IRA helps institutions prioritize their efforts to
manage the identified risks effectively.
1.11 Regular IRA enables institutions to protect and maintain the integrity
of their businesses while contributing to the integrity of the financial
system as a whole.
1.12 IRA must be:
1.12.1 Documented and a record maintained of its approval process
including formal approval by senior management and Board.
1.12.2 Regularly reviewed and updated.
1.12.3 Updated where risk inputs or factors change.
1.12.4 Reviewed and updated on an ongoing basis but at least
annually or where there are changes in the relevant laws and
material changes in the AML/CFT/CPF landscape, nationally
and internationally.
1.12.5 Conducted prior to the launch or use of new products, business
practices, delivery mechanisms and technological
developments.
1.12.6 Be made available to the Authority or Financial Reporting
Centre upon request.

2.0 Purpose of this Guidance Note
2.1 The purpose of this guidance note is to set out general principles to
enable reporting institutions to conduct ML, TF and PF institutional
risk assessment (IRA).
2.2 This note is for guidance purposes only and does not supersede or
replace any legal requirement and does not constitute any legal
advice and cannot be relied upon as evidence of complying with the
requirements of the relevant laws.
2.3 This guidance note should be read in conjunction with the relevant
laws and accompanying regulations.
3 | P age

3.0 General Requirements
3.1 IRA is the foundation of a proportionate AML compliance
framework.
3.2 An institution needs to put in place a policy and procedures for
conducting and reviewing ML, TF and PF risk assessment.
3.3 The ultimate responsibility for ensuring that the institution
conducts or reviews IRA lies with the institution’s Board of
Directors.
3.4 An institution should continuously identify ML, TF or PF risks at all
management levels, from the operational level to the Board, and to
include all the units of the institution.
3.5 The nature, scale and complexity of an institution is key in
determining how susceptible it is to be abused for ML, TF or PF.
3.5.1 Large institutions are less likely to know their customers
personally who can be more anonymous compared to
customers of small institutions.
3.5.2 Institutions that provide international services are more
susceptible to ML, TF or PF than domestic institutions.
3.6 An institution should conduct risk identification and analysis of all
existing and new products, activities and processes including use of
new technologies.
3.7 An institution should assess both the inherent ML/TF/PF risk,
residual risk as well as emerging ML/TF/PF risk.
3.8 An effective process of ML/TF/PF risk identification and analysis is
the basis for developing an adequate system of risk management
and control, thus enabling an institution to achieve its objective of
minimizing possible adverse effects arising from that risk.
3.9 An adequate and effective system of ML/TF/PF risk management
includes:
3.9.1 ML, TF and PF risk assessment of the business and its
customers.
3.9.2 Policies, procedures and controls to mitigate the identified ML,
TF and PF risks.
3.9.3 An organizational structure to execute risk management
controls.
3.9.4 A process to systematically assess compliance, adequacy,
appropriateness, effectiveness and implementation of risk
management systems.
3.10 An institution should be able to identify risks in a manner that
allows them to drill down into various risk factors to provide
qualitative information to ensure a robust risk assessment.
4 | P age

3.11 An institution should conduct separate ML, TF and PF risk
assessments, not combine the assessments.
3.12 An institution should periodically review, evaluate and update the
IRA as ML/TF/PF risks change and evolve over time with new
threats, products/services, new technologies, typologies, changes in
the law, updates on the National Risk Assessment (NRA) or Sectoral
Risk Assessment (SRA), etc.,

4.0 Risk Based Approach
4.1 A risk-based approach (RBA):
4.1.1 Recognizes that ML/TF/PF threats to an institution vary across
customers, countries, products and services, transactions and
distribution channels.
4.1.2 Allows an institution to apply appropriate and proportionate
measures to manage and mitigate the identified ML/TF/PF
risks based on the nature, scale and complexity of the
institution’s business and ML/TF/PF risk profile.
4.1.3 Facilitates effective allocation of the institution’s resources and
internal structures to manage and mitigate the identified
ML/TF/PF risks.
4.1.4 Facilitates determination of the degree of due care to be applied
to customers based on their risk profiles:
4.1.4.1 Low Risk Customers – Simplified due diligence (SDD).
4.1.4.2 Higher Risk Customers – Enhanced Customer due
diligence (ECDD).
4.1.5 Enables an institution to identify and assess potential gaps or
weaknesses of their AML compliance program.
4.2 An institution is required to:
4.2.1 Have good knowledge of its customers.
4.2.2 Understand transactions that are being conducted by the
customers.
4.2.3 Establish a monitoring mechanism to be adapted to a specific
level of customer risk.
4.3 An institution should incorporate RBA into its existing policies,
procedures and controls as part of its overall risk management.

5.0 Risk Assessment Methodology
5.1 While there is no prescribed methodology, the IRA is expected to
reflect material and foreseeable ML/TF/PF threats and
vulnerabilities which an institution is exposed to during the period
under review.
5.2 The risk assessment methodology should be tailored to the nature,
scale and complexity of the institution’s activities and operations.
5.3 An institution should utilize information from a variety of sources,
which can be accessed individually or through commercially
available tools or databases that pool information from several
sources.
5.4 An effective methodology should:
5.4.1 Consider input from internal sources, such as reports from the
compliance function, risk management and independent
reviews, as well as information from external sources, such as
the NRA, SRA, topical risk assessments, official guidance and
bodies such as the FATF.
5.4.2 Describe the selection and weighting of risk factors and reflect
the institution’s risk appetite.
5.4.3 Utilize both quantitative and qualitative data and information.
5.4.4 Make use of internal interviews, questionnaires, and
independent review reports, and provide for quality assurance
review.
5.4.5 Provide for separate, tailored assessments of different business
lines or segments that have different risk profiles before
consolidating into a unified view.
5.5 An institution should consider all relevant factors including:
5.5.1 Nature, scale and complexity of its business.
5.5.2 Products and services.
5.5.3 Customer types.
5.5.4 Delivery channels.
5.5.5 Geographical locations.
5.5.6 Institutions it engages with.
5.5.7 Applicable identified threats and vulnerabilities in the NRA and
SRA.
5.6 An institution should determine the model or method for risk
measurement taking into consideration:
5.6.1.1 nature, scale and complexity of its business activities.
5.6.1.2 the business needs e.g. for pricing.
5.6.1.3 assumptions of the methods or models.
5.6.1.4 data availability.
7 | P age

5.6.1.5 the sophistication of its management information system (MIS).
5.6.1.6 staff expertise.
5.7 The board and senior management of the institution need to
understand the underlying assumptions used and constraints of the
methods or models chosen and should be satisfied as to the
adequacy and appropriateness of the key assumptions, data
sources and procedures used to measure the risks.
5.8 An institution needs to verify the accuracy and reliability of the
chosen risk measurement method or model against the actual
results through regular back-testing and ensure that the method or
model is reviewed regularly in line with changing market conditions.
5.9 An institution needs to ensure that the chosen method or model for
risk assessment is relevant and easily understood by the parties
concerned.

6.0 Risk Assessment Process
6.1 An institution needs to ensure that the risk assessment provides a
comprehensive analysis of the ML/TF/PF risks in a concise and
organized manner and should be shared and communicated with
all business lines across the reporting institution, board of directors
and management.
6.2 The IRA should encompass the following at a minimum:
6.2.1 Identification and assessment of ML/TF/PF risks that may be
associated with the institution’s unique combination of
products and services, customers, geographic locations,
delivery channels and other factors.
6.2.2 An analysis of all available data.
6.2.3 An evaluation of the institution’s AML Compliance programme.
6.2.4 A determination of the residual risk for the risk categories
identified.
6.2.5 Use of appropriate weights and scoring.
6.2.6 Be specific to the institution and commensurate with the
nature and size of the institution’s business.
6.2.7 Be subjected to internal review and approval by the
management and board.
6.3 An institution should:
6.3.1 Document the risk assessment methodology in the AML policy
document.
6.3.2 Update AML compliance program at least every two years or
after the occurrence of a material event whichever comes
earlier.

7.1 Risk is a function of the likelihood of the occurrence of risk events
and the impact of the events.
7.1.1 Likelihood of occurrence is a combination of threat and
vulnerability i.e. risk events occur when a threat exploits
vulnerability.
7.1.2 The level of risk can be mitigated by minimizing the size of the
threats, vulnerabilities, or their impact.

7.2.2 Relationship-based risk assessment (RbRA) – This entails

8.0 Business-Based Risk Assessment
8.1 Business-based Risk Assessment (BbRA) is an assessment of the
risk of the institution being exploited for ML/TF/PF taking into
consideration the nature, scale and complexity of the institution,
the diversity of its operations (including geographical diversity), the
volume and size of transactions, and the degree of risk associated
with each area of its operations.
8.2 An institution should evaluate every segment of its business
operations to identify where a ML/TF/PF threat may emerge and
assess its vulnerability to that threat.
8.2.1.1 It is advisable to continually identify ML/TF/PF risks at all
management levels - from the operational level to the Executive
and the Board - and should include all organizational units.
8.3 An institution needs to conduct and document an assessment of its
overall exposure to risks to its organizational structure, its
corporate culture, its customers, the jurisdictions with which its
customers are connected, its products and services, and how it
delivers those products and services.
8.4 An institution need not only assess the risks that may expose it to
ML/TF/PF but also, corruption, violations of sanctions, regulations,
and tax evasion to be able to make informed decisions about the
risks that it is willing to take and the control measures to be taken.
8.5 The overall BbRA includes the risk posed by the following:
8.5.1 Combination of an institution’s products, services and delivery
channels.
8.5.2 Geographical locations in which the institution operates.
8.5.3 The impact of new developments, (e.g. new regulations, new
risks and threats), and new systems and technologies on the
institution’s operations.
8.5.4 Risks arising from affiliates and the activities that they
conduct.
8.5.5 Other relevant factors.
8.6 An institution may consider the following categories of business
risk:
8.6.1 Environmental Risk - This risk arises from the industry or
environment in which the institution is operating.
8.6.1.1 This risk is external to the institution and assesses the
institution’s vulnerability to predicate offences, ML, TF,
PF, targeted financial sanctions (TFS) and regulatory
compliance.
8.6.1.2 Each industry has a different level of exposure to
various predicate offences.
13 | P age

8.6.1.3 Other factors that have an impact on environmental
risk include locations on which the institution operates
and the type of customers in its portfolio.
8.6.2 Operational Risk – This is an internal risk and arises from the
way the institution conducts itself.
8.6.2.1 The level of operational risk can be affected by the
number of employees, outsourced activities, existence
of a compliance function and product development.
8.6.3 Product/Service Risk - This is the risk that arises from the
nature and attributes of the products/services an institution
offers.
8.6.3.1 Characteristics of products offered by an institution
significantly affect the level of ML/TF/PF risk that an
institution is exposed to.
8.6.3.2 Products that offer higher anonymity, cross-border
transactions, complex structures or those that
inherently have higher cash flows are considered
riskier.
8.6.4 Customer Risk – This is the risk that arises from the diverse
nature of customers that the institution is serving.
8.6.4.1 Factors such as customer’s background, occupation,
business activities, and the transparency of their source
of funds or wealth contribute to the risk profile.
8.6.4.2 High-risk customers might include politically exposed
persons (PEPs), those from countries with inadequate
AML controls or individuals involved in industries prone
to money laundering.
8.6.5 Delivery Risk – The channels used to deliver products / services
to customers affect the ML/TF/PF risk that the institution is
exposed to such as online and use of intermediaries.
8.6.6 Geographical Risk – These are risks associated with the
countries or regions in which the institution operates, as well
as those with which its customers have connections.
8.6.6.1 Countries with high levels of corruption, weak AML
regulations, known tax havens or those under
international sanctions are typically deemed higher
risk.
8.7 An institution needs to evaluate the likelihood and the extent of the

that affect their business and operations which may include the
following:

8.7.3 Risks associated with the legal structure of the institution,

8.13.1 Determines the level of risk the reporting institution is willing

which must be commensurate with the identified ML/TF/PF
risks.

11.0 Risk Analysis
11.1 After identifying and documenting all the inherent risks, an
institution evaluates the risk based on likelihood of the risk

11.2 An institution should conduct a detailed analysis of the data to
determine the nature, sources, likelihood and impact of the

11.2.1 The purpose is to get a holistic understanding of each of the

importance.
11.3 An institution should determine the level of ML/TF/PF risk
associated with a business relationship without considering the

11.3.1 In determining the level of ML/TF/PF risk, an institution

11.4 An institution should be able to demonstrate that it understands

reflects its understanding of these risks.
Risk Matrix Approach
11.5 One way to determine the level of ML/TF/PF risk is using a risk
matrix is by assessing the chance (likelihood) of the risk occurring
and the severity or amount of loss or damage (impact) which may
result should the risk materialize.
11.5.1 Likelihood is the probability of the presence of ML/TF/PF and
measures the level of risk an institution has identified as part
of the BbRA or RbRA.
11.5.2 Impact is the damage incurred if ML/TF/PF occurs and the
damage could be a financial loss, regulatory, legal or
reputational.
11.5.3 The higher a risk ranks for these two factors, the higher the
level of ML/TF/PF risk an institution is exposed to.
11.6 An institution needs to define both the likelihood scale and impact
scale.
11.6.1 Based on the nature, scale and complexity of the institution,
an institution can use 3 levels or 5 levels.

Risk Scoring Approach
11.11 Another way to determine the level of risk is to assign weights to the
risk factors based on their risk level.
11.12 There is no fixed or single approach to weighing the relative
importance of the risk factors; the institution should determine the
weighting or materiality for each factor under consideration which
individually or in combination may increase or decrease potential
ML/TF/PF risks posed to the institution.
11.12.1 Some risk factors are more important than others, so they
should receive a larger share of the score.
11.12.2 Improperly balanced weights could give a distorted picture of
the level of risk.
11.13 An institution should use informed judgement on the relevance of
the various risk factors in the context of a business relationship
when applying a weighting to each risk factor.
11.14 An institution should use a RBA when assigning weights to each of
the risk factors considering the nature, scale and complexity of its
business activities, products and services, client base and
geographic footprint.
11.14.1 Each risk factor is assigned a score which reflects the
associated level of risk, e.g. 1 – Lower Risk, 5 – Higher Risk.
11.14.2 Each risk area may be assigned a weight which reflects the level
of importance in the overall risk computation relative to other
risk areas, e.g. 1 – Limited Relevance; 2- Relevant; and 3 – Very
Relevant.
11.15 Weighting for each factor may vary based on the considered
importance of the impact of the factor on the institution’s business.
11.16 When weighting risk factors, an institution must ensure that:
11.16.1 The risk scoring model is in line with the legal requirement.
11.16.2 The risk scoring model considers the mandatory high-risk
situations for instance, an automatic high-risk score is
assigned to PEPs, customers registered in high-risk
jurisdictions, etc.
11.16.3 The weighting of the risk criteria is not unduly influenced by a
single factor.
11.16.4 Economic or profit considerations do not influence the
weighting.
11.16.5 Weighting does not lead to a situation where it is impossible for
any business relationship to be classified as high risk.
11.16.6 Situations identified by national legislation, NRAs or SRAs as
presenting a high ML, TF or PF risk are not rated lower than in
those assessments.
33 | P age

11.16.7 Where an override mechanism is used to alter a generated
score, the rationale for the decision to override the generated
score is documented and approved at senior management
and/or Board level.
11.16.8 There is a mechanism for:
11.16.8.1 Reviewing the individual customer on a regular basis or
when trigger events occur such as when the customer
wishes to take out a new product or service, when a
certain transaction threshold is reached, etc.
11.16.8.2 Adjusting customer re-scoring should there be material
changes risk scoring model or to components of the risk
scoring model including significant changes to the
geographical risk score due to external factors such as
inclusion of the country on the FATF grey or blacklist.
11.17 When using the risk scoring methodology, an institution should
consider the following four inherent risk factors:
11.17.1 Customer - Risks associated with the customer’s profile that
could increase the risk to the institution such as type of
customer (natural or legal), citizenship, PEP or other high-risk
customers.
11.17.2 Product and service risk factors - factors that relate to the
customer’s use of the institution’s products and services.
11.17.3 Geographical risk factors - Factors that relate to the
geographical location of the customer.
11.17.4 Delivery channels - risk scoring factors related to the channels
through which the institution’s products and services are
offered to the customer such as direct or indirect, face-to-face
versus non-face-to-face.

11.18 After identifying the risk factors in all the four categories, an
institution develops the risk spectrum for available scenarios and
determine their risk level.
11.18.1 For instance, does a customer who is a domestic PEP, who
lives and works in the same country, pose a higher ML/TF/PF
(or more specifically, bribery and corruption) risk as compared
to an international PEP who travels to different countries and
regions?
11.19 The final step is to assign appropriate weights/scores to the risk
factors and combine them into a single overall ML/TF/PF risk score.
11.20 An institution can generate the institutional risk by combining all
the inherent risks assessed for each category and indicators of risk.
36 | P age

12.0 Setting Risk Tolerance
12.1 The outcome of the risk assessment determines the level of risk an
institution is willing to accept i.e. the risk appetite and its
appropriate risk rating.
12.1.1 The risk appetite and risk rating will have a direct impact on
the proposed risk management and mitigation procedures,
systems and controls adopted by the reporting institution.
12.1.2 The risk appetite and the rating should be approved by the
Board and includes a risk appetite statement which should be
incorporated in the risk management policy and procedures
documentation.
12.2 An institution can consider the following factors when setting its
risk tolerance:
12.2.1 Regulatory risk.
12.2.2 Reputational risk.
12.2.3 Legal risk.
12.2.4 Financial risk.
12.3 An institution needs to clearly document the deviations that are
acceptable as well as where approving authority lies for exceeding
risk appetite thresholds i.e. an institution’s risk tolerance.
12.3.1 While risk appetite is often broad, risk tolerance is tactical,
quantitative, focused and applies to significant objectives and
cascades throughout the institution, providing guidance on a
daily basis.
12.3.2 An institution needs to consider the relative importance of each
objective when setting the risk tolerance - highly significant
objectives are often assigned low-risk tolerances.
12.3.3 Risk tolerance enables the institution to determine the level of
exposure (e.g. number of high-risk clients, inherently high-risk
products, etc.) to be accommodated when considering threats.
12.4 An institution should ensure that the risk assessment is reflected
in its policies and procedures and should justify the outcome of the
risk assessment.
37 | P age

13.0 Establish Controls and Assess Effectiveness
13.1 An institution shall develop and implement mitigation measures to
limit the ML/TF/PF risks that have been identified during the risk
assessment.
13.2 An institution might consider employing a three lines of defence
regime to ensure effective risk and control measures, namely:
13.2.1 First line roles deliver products/services to clients while
managing risk e.g. front office, customer-facing activity.
13.2.2 Second line roles deliver expertise, support, monitoring, and
challenge on risk related matters e.g. risk
management/compliance function.
13.2.3 Third line roles deliver independent and objective assurance
and advice on all related matters e.g. internal audit.
13.3 The mitigation measures include:
13.3.1 Governance and Board oversight.
13.3.2 Internal policies, procedures and controls as stipulated in
POCAMLA and accompanying Regulations.
13.3.3 Adequate screening procedures to ensure high standards when
hiring employees.
13.3.4 Ongoing training for employees, intermediaries and board
members.
13.3.5 Policies and procedures to prevent the misuse of technological
developments.
13.3.6 Mechanisms for preventing ML, TF or PF, or any other serious
offence.
13.3.7 Independent audit to review and verify compliance with and
effectiveness of the measures taken in accordance with
AML/CFT/CPF regime.
13.3.8 Risk based approach to managing identified ML, TF or PF risks.
13.3.9 Effective:
13.3.9.1 Customer identification procedures;
13.3.9.2 Record keeping and retention; and
13.3.9.3 Reporting procedures;
13.3.10 Confidentiality requirements and procedures.
13.3.11 Transaction monitoring systems.
13.3.12 Adequate screening procedures for customers against relevant
sanctions lists.
13.3.13 Enhanced identification, verification and ongoing due diligence
procedures with respect to customers who have been identified
as high-risk customers.

14.3.1 Any divergence in an institution’s overall residual risk rating,
as compared to sector-specific ratings in the NRA or equivalent,

14.3.2 The overall residual risk rating is used to indicate whether the
ML/TF/PF risks within the institution are being adequately
managed.
14.3.3 Using the RBA, an institution can apply a 3-tier rating scale or
a 5-point scale to determine the residual risk.

15.0 Risk Evaluation
15.1 An institution should identify priorities and create effective
strategies that align with the level of residual risks.
15.2 An institution should ensure that the residual risk is in line with
their overall risk tolerance i.e. the remaining risks do not exceed
what the institution can withstand.
15.3 Where the level of residual risk exceeds the overall tolerance; or the
measures and controls do not mitigate the high-risk situations or
customers sufficiently, the institution should increase the level
and/or quantity of mitigation measures that have been put in place.
44 | P age

16.0 Formulating Risk Response
16.1 Depending on the risk appetite, the institution employs techniques
to address identified risks.
16.2 The different responses to ML/TF risks can be summarised with the
4Ts of risk management: Tolerate, Terminate, Treat and Transfer.
Table 19 – Risk Response
16.3 Tolerate – A reporting institution might decide to retain the
enterprise risk where the likelihood and / or impact of the
ML/TF/PF risk is low.
16.3.1 This response is appropriate where the impact of ML/TF/PF is
within acceptable limits.
16.4 Terminate – An institution eliminates the probability of the risk
materialising by putting in place measures to stop and end the
activity that causes the specific risk such as exiting a product line,
certain market segment, selling a subsidiary, or deciding against
expansion.
16.4.1 An institution might decide to terminate the ML/TF/PF risks that
are outside its risk appetite limits or assessed as having a high
likelihood, impact or both.
16.4.2 This response is appropriate for the processes and activities that
create more significant ML/TF/PF risks compared to the benefits
should be terminated.
16.5 Treat - An institution mitigates its vulnerability to ML/TF/PF with
the aim of ensuring that the ensure that identified ML/TF/PF risks
are addressed through effective controls.
16.5.1 The measures are aimed at minimizing the likelihood or impact of
the risk, or both the likelihood of the risk happening and the
impact should it happen.
16.6 Transfer – An institution minimizes the likelihood and impact of the
ML/TF/PF risk by entering arrangements with third-party

17.0 Updating the Risk Assessment
23.1 An institution should put in place systems and controls to review
the BbRA and RbRA to ensure that their assessment of ML/TF/PF
risks remains up-to-date and relevant.
23.2 An institution must ensure changing, new or emerging risks can be
captured in the IRA and that the resources allocated to mitigate
identified risks remain proportionate to the risk level.
23.3 An institution must ensure that where a new risk has emerged, or
an existing risk has increased or decreased, it is reflected in the risk
assessment as soon as possible.
23.4 New risks include trigger events such as:
23.4.1 Emergence of new technology.
23.4.2 New customer base.
23.4.3 New services or products.
23.4.4 Entry into new geographic markets.
23.4.5 Suspicious activities / transaction reports.
23.4.6 Compliance failures.
23.4.7 Findings from audit reports and intelligence from staff.
23.4.8 New ML/TF/PF risks as identified by the FATF, ESAAMLG,
competent authorities or law enforcement agencies; or
23.4.9 Reviewed laws or regulations
23.5 An institution might consider reviewing the internal controls
following an elevation in the level of risk identified to ensure that
the controls remain appropriate to mitigate the elevated ML/TF/PF
risks.
23.6 When updating the risk assessment, an institution should consider
the identified threats and vulnerabilities from any MF/TF/PF risk
assessments conducted in the country to ensure that ML/TF/PF
risk inherent to the institution is understood at the national level
and is reflected in the IRA.
23.7 An institution should conduct and/or review their IRAs on an
annual basis due to the rate of change in risks.

INDICATORS OF SUSPICIOUS TRANSACTIONS
1. A request by a customer to enter into an insurance contract(s) where the source of
the funds is unclear or not consistent with the customer's apparent standing.
2. A sudden request for a significant purchase of a lump sum contract with an existing
customer whose current contracts are minimal and of regular payments only.
3. A proposal which has no discernible purpose and a reluctance to divulge a "need"
for making the investment.
4. A proposal to purchase and settle by cash.
5. A proposal to purchase by utilizing a cheque drawn from an account other than the
personal account of the proposer.
6. The prospective client who does not wish to know about investment performance
but does enquire on the early cancellation or surrender of the particular contract.
7. A customer establishes a large insurance policy and within a short time period
cancels the policy, requests the return of the cash value payable to a third party.
8. Early termination of a product, especially in a loss.
9. A customer applies for an insurance policy relating to business outside the
customer's normal pattern of business.
10. A customer requests for a purchase of insurance policy in an amount considered to
be beyond his apparent need.
11. A customer attempts to use cash to complete a proposed transaction when this type
of business transaction would normally be handled by cheques or other payment
instruments.
12. A customer refuses, or is unwilling, to provide explanation of financial activity, or
provides explanation assessed to be untrue.
13. A customer is reluctant to provide normal information when applying for an
insurance policy, provides minimal or fictitious information or, provides
information that is difficult or expensive for the institution to verify.
14. Delay in the provision of information to enable verification to be completed.
15. Opening accounts with the customer's address outside the local service area.
16. Opening accounts with names similar to other established business entities.
17. Attempting to open or operating accounts under a false name.
18. Any transaction involving an undisclosed party.
19. A transfer of the benefit of a product to an apparently unrelated third party.
20. A change of the designated beneficiaries (especially if this can be achieved without
knowledge or consent of the insurer or the right to payment could be transferred
simply by signing an endorsement on the policy).
21. Substitution, during the life of an insurance contract, of the ultimate beneficiary
with a person without any apparent connection with the policy holder.
22. The customer accepts very unfavourable conditions unrelated to his health or age.
23. An atypical incidence of pre-payment of insurance premiums.

180(cid:9) Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020
24. Insurance premiums have been paid in one currency and requests for claims to be
paid in another currency.
25. Activity is incommensurate with that expected from the customer considering the
information already known about the customer and the customer's previous
financial activity. For individual customers, consider customer's age, occupation,
residential address, general appearance, type and level of previous financial activity.
For corporate customers, consider type and level of activity.
26. Any unusual employment of an intermediary in the course of some usual
transaction or formal activity e.g. payment of claims or high commission to an
unusual intermediary.
27. A customer appears to have policies with several institutions.
28. A customer wants to borrow the maximum cash value of a single premium policy,
soon after paying for the policy.
29. The customer who is based in non-co-operative countries designated by the
Financial Action Task Force from time to time or in countries where the production
of drugs or drug trafficking may be prevalent.
30. The customer who is introduced by an overseas agent, affiliator or other company
that is based in non-co-operating countries designated by the Financial Action Task
Force from time to time or in countries where corruption or the production of drugs
or drug trafficking may be prevalent.
31. A customer who is based in Kenya and is seeking a lump sum investment and offers
to pay by a wire transaction or foreign currency.
32. Unexpected changes in employee characteristics including a lavish lifestyle or
avoiding taking holidays.
33. Unexpected change in employee or agent performance, e.g. the sales person selling
products has a remarkable or unexpected increase in performance.
34. Consistently high activity levels of single premium business far in excess of any
average company expectation.
35. The use of an address which is not the client's permanent address, e.g. utilization of
the salesman's office or home address for the dispatch of customer documentation.
36. Any other indicator as may be detected by the insurance institutions from time to
time.

Chairman,

IN EXERCISE of the powers conferred by section 180 of the
Insurance Act, the Cabinet Secretary for the National Treasury and
Planning makes the following regulations —
1. These Regulations may be cited as the Insurance (Group- Citation.
Wide Supervision) Regulations, 2020.
2. In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires — Interpretation.
"Act" means the Insurance Act; Cap. 487.
"financial conglomerate" means a group of companies including
an insurance group of companies, whether operating or non-operating,
under common control or dominant influence, comprised of a financial
holding company which conducts material financial activities in at least
two of the regulated financial services sectors and includes an un-
regulated entity;
"parent company" means the entity which controls or exerts
dominant influence over a financial conglomerate and may be the
ultimate parent or the head of a conglomerate that is a subset of the
wider group;
"unregulated entity" means an entity that is not directly regulated
by a financial sector regulator; and
"wider group" means the group to which a financial
conglomerate belongs including where the financial conglomerate is
part of a larger diversified conglomerate with both financial and non-
financial entities.
3. The objective of these regulations is to — Objective of the
regulations.
(a) address regulatory arbitrage from group activities and ensure
effective supervision of group risks; and
(b) ensure that supervision has proper regard to all entities which
may affect the overall risk profile and financial position of
the group or the individual entities within the group.

title: Microinsurance Regulations, 2020 (LN NO. 26)
text:
192(cid:9) Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020
LEGAL NOTICE No. 26
THE INSURANCE ACT
(Cap. 487)
THE INSURANCE (MICROINSURANCE) REGULATIONS, 2020
IN EXERCISE of the powers conferred by section 180 of the
Insurance Act, the Cabinet Secretary for the National Treasury and
Planning makes the following regulations —
1. These Regulations may be cited as the Insurance Citation.
(Microinsurance) Regulations, 2020.
2. In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires— (cid:9) Interpretation.
"bundled microinsurance product" means a microinsurance
product that covers one or more classes of—
(a) general insurance business;
(b) long term insurance business; and
(c) general and long-term insurance business;
"general microinsurance product" means a health insurance
contract, a contract covering personal belongings including dwellings,
livestock, crops or tools of trade, or a personal accident contract, either
on individual or group basis, according to the terms specified in the
microinsurance criteria of the contract;
"fixed sum insurance" means an insurance contract under which
an agreed specified fixed sum is payable or agreed specified fixed
benefits shall be provided by the insurer to the policyholder on the
occurrence of the insured risk regardless of the actual loss or damage
suffered by the policyholder;
"grace period" means a specified period immediately following
the premium due date during which a payment can be made to continue
a policy in force without interruption;
"life microinsurance product" means a life insurance product
feigned in accordance with terms stated in the microinsurance criteria;
"master policyholder" in relation to a group microinsurance
Al.T -ac, means a person who is the legal holder of the policy issued in
of that contract;
-microinsurer" means a person registered under the Act to carry
nacroinsurance business;
"microinsurance business" means insurance that is accessed by or
accessible to the low-income population, including the underserved
markets provided by a variety of different entities and managed in
accordance with generally accepted insurance principles;
"microinsurance actuary" means a person who holds the
qualifications of Certified Actuarial Analyst at a minimum; and
"waiting period" means the period an insured person shall be
required to wait before some or all of that person's insurance coverage
shall come into effect.

ubsidiary Legislation, 2020(cid:9) 193
3. Save as specifically provided, these regulations shall apply Scope of the
to any person engaged in microinsurance business. regulations.
4. (1) The grace period for microinsurance contracts shall be at Grace periods.
least forty-five days from the date when the premium falls due for
payment.
(2) A grace period shall not be provided for index-based
microinsurance products.
5. A microinsurance contract shall satisfy the following microinsurance
criteria— (cid:9) criteria.
(a) the policy shall offer protection to an individual or members
of a group and their property and shall exclude third party
liability risks;
(b) the contract term of the policy shall not exceed twelve
months;
(c) the policy may be renewable at the end of the contract term
without the need for a new policy document subject to the
payment of premium;
(d) the amount of daily premiums or contributions shall not
exceed forty shillings;
(e) the sum insured shall not be more than five hundred
thousand shillings;
(t) the policy shall be a fixed sum insurance contract;
(g) the policy shall not provide for a change of the product's
features during the term of the contract;
(h) the policy shall expressly state that the cover under the
contract shall not commence until —
(i) the premium has been paid; or
(ii) where the contract provides for payment of the premium
by instalments, the first instalment of the premium has
been paid.
6. (1) A microinsurer shall apply to the Authority for approval Approval of
of a microinsurance product and any amendments to the terms of the microinsurance
product in accordance with the product approval guidelines issued products.
under the Act.
(2) In addition to the conditions specified in paragraph (1), a
microinsurer shall submit —
(a) a sample policy summary;
(b) the proposed commission rates or fee structures;
(c) a sales plan specifying how the product will be marketed and
distributed; and
(d) copies of drafts of any agreements with intermediaries or
other persons who shall be involved in the marketing or
distribution of the product.
7. (1) The Authority may, by notice in writing, revoke the Revocation of
approval of a microinsurance product— (cid:9) approval of
microinsurance
products.

194(cid:9) Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020
(a) on application by the microinsurer;
(b) where the product ceases to meet the requirements of the Act
or these regulations; or
(c) where the microinsurer ceases to comply with the provisions
of the Act or these regulations.
(2) A revocation of approval of an existing microinsurance
product shall not affect any existing contracts.
8. (1) A microinsurer shall not alter the microinsurance product's Change of product
features without the prior written approval of the Authority. features.
(2) An application to change the microinsurance product's
features shall be accompanied by a written certification by the
microinsurance actuary that the revised terms have been determined in
accordance with generally accepted actuarial methodologies.
(3) A change in the microinsurance product's features shall not
be applicable to existing contracts.
9. (1) A microinsurer may offer a group policy that meets the Group
following conditions — (cid:9) microinsurance
policies.
(a) the master policyholder purchases the insurance policy on
behalf of members of the group and their beneficiaries;
(b) the group is identifiable and exists independently of the
insurance contract;
(c) the group is not formed by an intermediary or a registered
insurer; and
(d) the risks insured under the policy are related to the common
interests or activities of the beneficiaries.
(2) Where group underwriting is applied, price discrimination
shall not be allowed between individuals within the group.
(3) The master policyholder shall disclose the premium payable
by each member of the group and the benefits payable to the members
at the inception of the contract.
10. Any marketing material developed for a microinsurance Marketing
contract shall be in the same language as the policy document and shall materials.
be in a clear, plain and easy to understand language.
11. (1) A microinsurer shall prepare a simple policy summary Policy summaries.
for each of its micro insurance policies with an express declaration in
the summary that the product is a microinsurance product.
(2) A policy summary shall —
(a) be no more than one A4 page with a minimum font size of
12 or in an electronic format that captures similar details that
it will have if it was in paper form;
(b) be written in clear, plain and easy to understand language
with no or minimal use of technical and legal language;
(c) where any technical or legal language is used, the language
shall be fully explained;
(d) be in the same language as the policy document; and
(e) contain a summary of the cover provided and the key
features of the policy.

Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020(cid:9) 195
(3) The policy summary shall be issued to prospective
policyholders, in electronic form or otherwise, prior to selling the
policy.
(4) Despite paragraph (2), the policy summary shall contain the
following information —
(a) the name of the microinsurer and the address of its principal
office in Kenya;
(b) a description of the insured risks and any exclusions or
limitations that apply;
(c) the duration of the policy, the period of cover, the grace
period and any waiting periods that apply;
(d) the principal benefits provided under the policy;
(e) any obligations on a prospective policyholder to disclose
material facts before purchasing the policy;
(f) procedures for payment of premiums, date when premium is
payable, amount of premium payable including
consequences of non-payment of premiums;
(g) whether, and in what circumstances the policy is renewable
and the procedures for renewal;
(h) whether, and in what circumstances the policy is renewable
and the procedures for renewal;
(i) the claims procedures;
(j) the right to complain and the method of lodging a complaint;
(k) a statement that the Policy Summary does not contain the
full terms of the insurance policy, which are to be found in
the policy document; and
(I) how the policyholder may obtain a copy of the policy
document.
12. (1) A microinsurer shall ensure that the policy document for Policy documents.
a microinsurance contract —
(a) is written in clear, plain and easy to understand language
with no, or minimal, use of technical and legal language; and
(b) will be easily understood by any person to whom it is
marketed and sold.
(2) A microinsurance policy document shall —
(a) be written in English or Kiswahili or any other language:
Provided that where a language other than English or
Kiswahili is used, the issuer shall provide an English or
Kiswahili translation of the microinsurance policy document;
(b) state in clear terms that it is a microinsurance policy;
(c) contain no or few exclusions; and
(d) shall specify —
(i) the name of the microinsurer;
(ii) the name of the policyholder;
(iii) the insured risk;

196(cid:9) Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020
(iv) the compensation to be made, or the benefits to be
provided, on the occurrence of the insured risk;
(v) any exclusions applicable to the contract; and
(vi) the procedure for making a claim.
13. (1) A microinsurer shall, within three working days of the Provision of
commencement of a microinsurance contract, provide the policyholder policy documents
with a policy document and a confirmation of receipt of premium. and receipts.
(2) A microinsurer may provide the documents under paragraph
(1) in electronic form.
14. (1) A microinsurer shall, within ten calendar days of receipt Claims payments.
of a claim notification under a microinsurance policy, pay or reject the
claim and, in the case of a rejection, notify the claimant in writing the
reasons for the rejection.
(2) Where a claim notification is received by a microinsurance
intermediary, such notification shall be deemed to have been received
by the microinsurer.
(3) Where a microinsurer is unable to complete the claim process
due to a reasonable cause, the microinsurer shall seek an extension of
time of not more than ten calendar days from the Authority to complete
the claims process.
15. (1) Except as otherwise provided for under the Act, only a Registration
person registered in accordance with these regulations shall carry on requirements.
microinsurance business in Kenya.
(2) The name of a registered microinsurer shall contain the word
"microinsurance" in microinsurer's registered name.
(3) A registered insurer who intends to carry on microinsurance
business shall set up a separate microinsurance company for that
purpose.
(4) Where a registered insurer sets up a separate microinsurance
company for the purposes of carrying on microinsurance business, the
management and governance structure of the parent company may be
used for the separate microinsurance company.
16. (1) Microinsurance registration applications shall be subject Application for
to similar registration requirements as insurers under the Act, but with registration.
capital, annual registration and operational requirements as set out in
these regulations.
(2) A person who has applied to be registered as a microinsurer
shall have the higher of —
(a) a minimum paid up capital of fifty million shillings; or
(b) risk-based capital as may be determined by the Authority.
(3) A microinsurer shall apply to the Authority for the renewal of
registration annually on or before the 30t" of September.
(4) The reserving requirements for microinsurance products
marketed or sold under by a microinsurer shall be the same as for
products sold under general insurance business.
17. (1) A microinsurer shall establish and maintain a function Complaints.
and procedures for dealing with enquiries, complaints and disputes.

Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020(cid:9) 197
(2) A microinsurer shall within seven calendar days of receiving
a complaint, resolve the complaint and notify the complainant of its
decision.
18. (1) A microinsurer may appoint a microinsurance Appointment of
intermediary by entering into an agreement which shall specify the microinsurance
terms and conditions of the relationship between the microinsurer and intermediaries.
the intermediary.
(2) A microinsurance intermediary shall not require to be
registered by the Authority.
(3) A microinsurer may appoint any person as a microinsurance
intermediary:
Provided that —
(a) the microinsurer is satisfied that the person is fit and proper
to be a microinsurance intermediary;
(b) the person has successfully completed a microinsurance
training program approved by the Authority; and
(c) the person shall be monitored and supervised as a
microinsurance intermediary by the microinsurer.
19. (1) A microinsurer shall keep and maintain a register of all Register of
microinsurance intermediaries that it has appointed. microinsurance
intermediaries.
(2) The register of microinsurance intermediaries shall include —
(a) full name, business address and contact details of each
intermediary;
(b) the date of appointment and termination where applicable;
(c) the volume of business generated by the microinsurance
intermediary by class or type;
(d) the source of microinsurance business; and
(e) the amount of commissions or fees paid to the
microinsurance intermediary.
20. (1) A microinsurer shall, at its expense, provide at least Training
twenty-five hours of training to all its microinsurance intermediaries at obligations.
the time of appointment.
(2) A microinsurer shall, at its expense, ensure that its
microinsurance intermediaries undergo refresher training of at least
fifteen hours after every three years.
(3) A microinsurance training programme shall include training
on —
(a) the provisions of the Act and these regulations;
(b) the duties and responsibilities of the intermediary in the
distribution of microinsurance products;
(c) the specific microinsurance products that the intermediary
shall be authorised to distribute;
(d) the insurance market;
(e) claims and complaints handling procedures of the
microinsurer; and

198(cid:9) Kenya Subsidiary Legislation, 2020
(f) consumer protection and the fair treatment of policyholders.
21. The commission or fee payable to a microinsurance Commissions and
intermediary by the microinsurer shall not exceed fifteen per cent of the fees.
premium paid.
22. In addition to any other reporting requirements under the Reporting
Act, a microinsurer shall regularly report to the Authority on the requirements.
following matters —
(a) information in respect of microinsurance business as may be
required by the Authority;
(b) quarterly information regarding the handling of complaints
or grievances made against the microinsurer or its
microinsurance intermediaries not more than fifteen days
after the end of the quarter to which it relates; and
(c) annual reports on microinsurance intermediaries that were
appointed by the microinsurer during the year not later than
three months after the end of the year in which the
appointments were made.
23. All the penalties and sanctions applicable to insurers under Enforcement.
the Act shall apply to microinsurers with the necessary modifications.
24. A registered insurer engaged in microinsurance business Transition.
shall continue providing such products and regularise compliance with
these regulations within three years from the date of the coming into
operation of these regulations.
Dated the 7th February, 2020.
UKUR YATANI,
Cabinet Secretary,
for National Treasury and Planning.
